fixes.explanation: Farmland doesn't make their lament. They lament her as “…city of renown inhabited by seafaring men—she who was powerful on the sea…” (Ezekiel 26:17). The princes remember her on the water.

False is right, baker. God says He will bring her down “…so that you will no longer be inhabited or set in splendor in the land of the living.” (Ezekiel 26:20). She will no longer be inhabited. She will no longer be set in splendor either.

Nobody in this verse is packing a care package. Tyre says, “Aha! The gate to the nations is broken…” (Ezekiel 26:2). That sounds like a city counting what it might gain, and I think that's the problem.
No gates are slamming in this verse. Tyre says the gate to the nations “…has swung open to me…” (Ezekiel 26:2). Tyre also says “…I will be filled…” so I think it's expecting to gain.

God doesn't take Tyre's side. He says, “Behold, O Tyre, I am against you…” (Ezekiel 26:3). Then He says He will raise up many nations against her. First Tyre says “Aha!” and then God says He is against her.

God says, “They will destroy the walls of Tyre and demolish her towers.” (Ezekiel 26:4). The walls and the towers both get the same treatment. Waves don't ask permission, and neither do these nations.

Sennacherib, king of Assyria (2 Kings 18:13), is a different royal from the one in this verse. God names Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon (Ezekiel 26:7). It's a good guess to mix up two big-name kings. Still, the text has its own name, and I'd stick with it.

Cyrus, king of Persia (Ezra 1:1), isn't the name in this verse. God says, “Behold, I will bring against Tyre from the north Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon…” (Ezekiel 26:7). Same kind of title, different king. Check the name and you're set.

God says, “He will direct the blows of his battering rams against your walls…” (Ezekiel 26:9). Rams, plural, so he isn't knocking politely. The verse before it has him build a ramp to her walls and raise his shields, and the rams are what he aims at those walls.
No ladders get mentioned here. God says, “He will direct the blows of his battering rams against your walls…” (Ezekiel 26:9). The verse has the blows of battering rams aimed at the walls.
God says, “…your walls will shake from the noise of cavalry, wagons, and chariots.” (Ezekiel 26:10). The walls shake from the noise. That's a LOUD army, friend.

It is true, so this one slips by. God says that when Nebuchadnezzar enters Tyre's gates, “…your walls will shake from the noise of cavalry, wagons, and chariots.” (Ezekiel 26:10). The text puts the shaking right on that noise.

God says they will “…throw your stones and timber and soil into the water.” (Ezekiel 26:12). Tyre sits in the sea, so I think the water is right there waiting. In the same verse He says they will demolish her walls and tear down her beautiful homes.
A plain isn't mentioned. God says they will “…throw your stones and timber and soil into the water.” (Ezekiel 26:12). The text names stones, timber and soil, and the water is where they go.

No rescue fleet shows up in this verse. God says the princes of the sea “…will descend from their thrones, remove their robes, and strip off their embroidered garments.” (Ezekiel 26:16). Instead the verse has them sit on the ground, trembling.

Nobody is throwing a party in this verse. God says the princes will sit on the ground, “…trembling every moment, appalled over you.” (Ezekiel 26:16). Then they lament for her, which is the opposite of celebrating.

God says, “…when I raise up the deep against you so that the mighty waters cover you…” (Ezekiel 26:19). Tyre sits in the sea, so the waters come right to her door. The city described as powerful on the sea gets covered by the mighty waters.
God says, “You will be sought, but will never be found…” (Ezekiel 26:21). That is a heavy word, friend. God declares that Tyre will be no more.
Even ruins don't turn up in this verse. God says, “You will be sought, but will never be found…” (Ezekiel 26:21). She is sought and never found. That is what the Lord GOD declares.
